title: Reading Data Tables
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Locating values, comparing rows and columns, and doing the arithmetic a table question needs

introduction.overview: A data table arranges numbers in rows and columns under headings. Table-based data interpretation (DI) questions ask you to read a value, compare values, and then use simple arithmetic such as totals, differences, averages, ratios and percentages. The skill is not hard mathematics but careful reading: finding the right row and the right column, noticing the units, and choosing the shortest calculation.
introduction.placementRelevance: Table-based DI sets are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually as a table followed by four or five questions. They reward accuracy and a calm, methodical approach.
introduction.realWorldContext: Placement reports, sales sheets, exam results and bank statements are all tables. Reading them correctly is a daily skill for engineers and analysts.

learningObjectives: Locate a value at the intersection of a row and a column
Find totals, differences and averages across rows and columns
Compute percentage change, percentage of total and ratios from table values
Use approximation to save time where options allow it

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Percentage of total = part ÷ total × 100. Average = sum ÷ count. Ratio a : b is simplified by dividing both terms by their HCF.

coreDefinitions: Row: a horizontal line of values (all values for one year, say). Column: a vertical line of values (all values for one branch, say).
Cell: the single value where a row and a column meet.
Heading and unit: the label of a row or column and the unit of its values (students, ₹ lakh, tonnes).
Total: the sum of the values in a row or column. Difference: one value minus another.
Percentage increase or decrease: the change between two values expressed as a percentage of the earlier value.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A table question is a three-step process: (1) read the question and decide which cells are needed, (2) pick up only those numbers, (3) do the shortest calculation. Skimming the whole table first for a "feel" for its size is useful, but computing everything in advance is a waste of time.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Put one finger on the row heading and another on the column heading and slide them together until they meet. Say the value aloud, with its unit, before doing any arithmetic.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Reading a cell
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Match the heading and the year or category exactly.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Totals and averages
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Total = sum of values;  Average = Total ÷ number of values
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Check that you use the right number of values.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Percentage change
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The base is the earlier value.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Ratio
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: a : b simplified by their HCF

mainNarrative: Always read the title and the units first. A table of "students placed" and a table of "salary in ₹ lakh" can look alike, but the arithmetic and the interpretation differ. If a column says "in thousands", then every value must be multiplied by 1000 when a question asks for the actual number.

To answer a question, find only the cells that matter. "Total students placed in 2022" needs one row; "Highest value for CSE" needs one column; "Increase in ECE between 2021 and 2024" needs two cells of the same column. Reading the question twice often saves more time than any shortcut.

Percentages from tables follow two patterns. Percentage change uses the earlier value as the base: the CSE count rose from 120 to 165, so the increase is 45 ÷ 120 × 100 = 37.5%. Percentage of total uses the total as the base: in 2022 the civil branch placed 50 out of 340 students, which is about 14.7%.
Many options are close together, which allows approximation. If the options for 150 ÷ 363 × 100 are 38.1, 41.3, 43.5 and 45.0, a rough calculation (150 ÷ 360 ≈ 0.42) is enough to choose 41.3.

Common traps are mixing rows and columns, using the wrong base in a percentage, and forgetting the unit. When your answer looks unusual (for example more than 100% for a share), recheck the cells you used.

deepDiveAspects.title: Comparing growth across rows
deepDiveAspects.content: Absolute increase and percentage increase can rank the rows differently. CSE grew by 45 students and CIVIL by 7, so CSE has the larger absolute growth; the percentage growth is 37.5% versus 15.6%. Read the question to know which one is asked for.

deepDiveAspects.title: Checking totals as a safety step
deepDiveAspects.content: If a table includes a total row or column, use it to verify your reading of individual cells. If the numbers do not add up, you may have misread a value.

problemVariations.description: Mean of a row or column.

solvedExamples.title: Total of a row
solvedExamples.question: Using the table of students placed, find the total number of students placed in 2022.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: A total is the sum of all values in the row.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Adding in pairs makes the sum easy to check.

solvedExamples.title: Percentage change
solvedExamples.question: By what percentage did CSE placements increase from 2021 to 2024?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The base is the earlier value, 120.

solvedExamples.title: Percentage of a total
solvedExamples.question: What percentage of the students placed in 2022 belonged to CIVIL (to one decimal place)?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The total of the row is the base.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Using a column total instead of the row total.

shortcutMethods.title: Pick-only-what-you-need

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Compute the total of every row and column before reading the questions.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Read the question first, pick up only the cells it needs, and use approximation when the options are far apart. Keep a small side note for any total you compute, because later questions often reuse it.

rulesForApplication: Read the title, units and headings before the questions.
Percentage change uses the old value as the base; percentage of total uses the total.
Round numbers to make a rough check against the options.
Reuse totals you have already worked out.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the wrong row or column
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Moving the finger a line too far.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Say the row and column headings aloud before reading the value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the wrong base for a percentage
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Dividing by the new value or by the wrong total.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Decide whether the question asks for change (old base) or share (total base).
Note the unit at the top of the table before calculating.
Add in pairs and cross-check with the totals if given.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Use approximation: round the values and compare with the options before doing exact arithmetic.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Do the direct-reading questions first, then the percentage and ratio ones.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: The data is always right in front of you; accuracy of reading is the main skill being tested.

summaryBullets: Read title, units and headings first.
Percentage change: old base. Percentage of total: total base.
Approximate when options are far apart.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I compute the percentage increase between two cells?
Can I find the share of one cell in its row total?
Can I simplify the ratio of two cells?
